chunks: "It depends on the priorities and the architecture. On a Cortex-M, the interrupt controller compares the new request's priority with the priority of the ISR currently running.
If the new one has a higher priority, the hardware preempts: it stacks another frame and runs the new ISR inside the first, and when it finishes it returns into the first ISR.
That's nesting. If the new one has the same or lower priority, it just waits as pending until the current ISR returns, and then runs, often via tail-chaining.
And the same interrupt can't preempt itself: if the same source fires again while its ISR runs, it gets latched as pending and runs again afterwards, though if it fired twice you only get one.
On an AVR, the hardware clears the global interrupt flag on entry, so nothing can interrupt an ISR unless I explicitly turn interrupts back on inside it, which I'd avoid.
Nesting reduces latency for urgent events but costs stack, adds shared-data hazards, and can lose events if an ISR is held up.
To control it, I'd set priorities deliberately: urgent ones high, everything else equal or in a few levels.
Keep ISRs short so overlaps are rare, mask the source or use BASEPRI around shared data, never re-enable interrupts inside a handler without a plan, and size the stack for the worst-case nest."
